title: Bigger Than You Think
covers: estimating, then finding, a whole number divided by a fraction, by counting how many pieces fit or multiplying by the reciprocal, and checking by multiplying
cert: estimating and dividing whole numbers by fractions, and checking by multiplying

intro.caption: Lesson 6-9 — dividing whole numbers by fractions. The academy's Supply Relay is not about speed. At each checkpoint, a team must ESTIMATE first and then compute. A good estimate earns the points. Three reader gates and a boss checkpoint stand between the cadets and the finish.

balloons.t: Relay rules: at every checkpoint, we estimate first. Then we compute. Then we check.
Points for thinking. Terrible news for Teo.
Dividing always makes things smaller. So the answer is tiny. That's classified.
Is it? We cut 8 meters into ¼-meter clips. Each meter makes 4 clips.

pages.caption: Dividing by a fraction less than 1 asks: how many small pieces fit? The answer can be bigger than the number you started with.

balloons.t: 8 meters of cable. Clips are ¼ meter each. Estimate first.
More or less than 8? No take-backs.
9 kilograms of gear. Each pack holds ¾ kilogram.
¾ is between ½ and 1. That gives you a range.
10 ÷ ⅖ = 4. Small answer, like I said. Classified.
⅖ is less than 1. My estimate says MORE than 10. Let's check.
Your team estimates. My team just knows. That's why we're ahead.
Then you know 4 liters is only ⅔ of that tank?
32 clips. 12 packs. A full tank. Bigger than Teo thought.

win.caption: Dividing a whole number by a fraction less than 1 gives an answer BIGGER than the whole number, because you count how many small pieces fit. Estimate first, multiply by the reciprocal, then check by multiplying.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Checkpoint Cable
gates.prompt: Cut 8 meters of cable into ¼-meter clips. Estimate first, then find 8 ÷ ¼.
hints: Conceptual: dividing by ¼ asks how many quarters fit in 8. Each piece is small, so many pieces fit.
Procedural: each meter holds 4 quarter-meters. Multiply the meters by 4. That is the same as multiplying by the reciprocal of ¼.

steps: Practice: 3 ÷ ⅕. Estimate: ⅕ is less than 1, so more than 3 pieces fit.
Each whole holds 5 fifths, so 3 wholes hold 3 × 5 = 15 fifths.
Check: 15 × ⅕ = 3. The estimate was right: 15 is more than 3.
worked.q: Estimate first: is 7 ÷ ½ more or less than 7? Then find it.

options.fb: That's the small-answer trap. Each clip is less than 1 meter, so MORE than 8 clips fit.
You get 8 only when you divide by 1. Each clip is just ¼ meter, so more fit.

items.label: 8 ÷ ¼ =
items.aria: number of one quarter meter clips in 8 meters

fb.msg: 2 is 8 × ¼, or 8 ÷ 4. Your estimate said MORE than 8. Count how many quarters fit.
12 is 8 + 4. Each of the 8 meters holds 4 clips, so multiply: 8 × 4.
That's ¼ ÷ 8, the order flipped. The cable is what gets cut up.

items.fbDefault: Each meter makes 4 clips. How many clips from 8 meters?

gates.pass: 32 clips, and the estimate said more than 8. Farah hands Teo the cutters. He cuts slowly.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Heavy Packs
gates.badge: Range Finder — Dividing by a Non-Unit Fraction
gates.prompt: Pack 9 kg of gear into packs of ¾ kg. Estimate a range, then find 9 ÷ ¾.
hints: Conceptual: ¾ is between ½ and 1. Dividing by 1 gives 9. Dividing by ½ gives twice as many. The answer is between them.
Procedural: multiply by the reciprocal. Flip ¾ to 4/3, then multiply 9 × 4/3.

steps: Practice: 6 ÷ ⅔. ⅔ is between ½ and 1, so the answer is between 6 and 12.
Check: 9 × ⅔ = 18/3 = 6. And 9 is between 6 and 12.

options.fb: Each pack holds less than 1 kg, so MORE than 9 packs are needed.
½-kg packs would make 18. These packs are bigger than ½ kg, so FEWER than 18 fit.

items.label: 9 ÷ ¾ =
items.aria: number of three quarter kilogram packs from 9 kilograms

fb.msg: That's 9 × ¾, which is less than 9. Multiply by the reciprocal, 4/3, instead.
36 is 9 ÷ ¼. Each pack holds THREE quarters, so put the 36 quarters in groups of 3.
27 is 9 × 3. Flip ¾ to 4/3: multiply by 4, then divide by 3.

gates.pass: 12 packs, right inside the range. Ozzie zips the last one and calls it a perfect landing.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Teo's Shortcut
gates.prompt: Teo says 10 ÷ ⅖ = 4. Use an estimate to judge it, fix it, then prove the fix.
hints: Conceptual: ⅖ is less than 1, so the answer must be more than 10. Any answer under 10 fails the estimate.
Procedural: multiply by the reciprocal, 5/2. Then check: the answer times ⅖ must give back 10.

steps: Practice: Vale says 6 ÷ ¾ = 4.5. Estimate: ¾ is less than 1, so the answer is more than 6. 4.5 fails.
Check: 8 × ¾ = 24/4 = 6. It lands back on 6.
worked.a: Yes. The answer times the divisor gives back 4.

options.t: Yes. Dividing makes the answer smaller.
options.fb: That's the trap. ⅖ is less than 1, so more than 10 pieces fit.

options.t: No. Dividing 10 by a fraction less than 1 gives more than 10.

options.fb: 4 × ⅖ = 8/5, which is less than 2. It does not give back 10.

fb.msg: 4 is 10 × ⅖. That is Teo's answer. Multiply by the reciprocal, 5/2.
5 is 10 ÷ 2. You used only the top of ⅖.
50 is 10 ÷ ⅕. Each piece is TWO fifths, so only half as many fit.

options.fb: That is Teo's shortcut again. It does not use your answer, 25.
Multiply the answer by the divisor, ⅖, not by the starting number.
A check multiplies back. 25 ÷ ⅖ is 62½, not 10.

gates.pass: The scanner beeps: 25 × ⅖ = 10. Teo stares at it. "The shortcut," he says, "is now classified."

gates.title: Boss Gate · The Drone Tank
gates.prompt: 4 liters of fuel fill ⅔ of the drone's tank. How much fills the whole tank? Estimate first.
hints: Conceptual: 4 liters is only part of the tank. The whole tank holds more. 4 ÷ ⅔ asks how much is in ONE whole.
Procedural: 4 liters is 2 thirds, so one third holds 4 ÷ 2. The whole tank is 3 thirds. Or multiply 4 × 3/2.

steps: Practice: 3 cups fill ¾ of a jar. How much fills the whole jar? That is 3 ÷ ¾.
3 cups is 3 quarters, so one quarter holds 1 cup. The whole jar is 4 quarters: 4 cups.
worked.q: 6 meters of tape is ⅓ of a roll. How long is the whole roll?

items.q: Estimate first. The whole tank holds…

options.fb: The 4 liters fill only ⅔ of the tank. The whole tank needs more.
4 liters would fill the WHOLE tank. Here they fill only ⅔ of it.

items.label: 4 ÷ ⅔ = liters in a full tank:
items.aria: liters in a full drone tank

fb.msg: That's 4 × ⅔, less than 4. Your estimate said more than 4.
2 liters fill just ONE third. The whole tank is three thirds.
12 treats 4 liters as one third. 4 liters is TWO thirds, so one third is 2 liters.

items.fbDefault: 4 liters is 2 thirds. Find one third, then three thirds.

items.q: Last check. Which divisions give an answer bigger than the number you start with? Select all that apply.

options.fb: ⅞ is less than 1, so the answer is more than 7. It is 8.
Dividing by 2 makes 3, which is smaller than 6. 2 is more than 1.
⅓ is less than 1, so the answer is more than 5. It is 15.
Dividing by 1 gives 6, the same number. Not bigger.

items.fbMiss: Look again. Every divisor less than 1 makes a bigger answer.
items.fbExtra: One of those divides by 1 or more. That answer is not bigger.

gates.pass: 6 liters exactly. The drone lifts off and the relay is done. Vale says she was about to estimate.

journal.heading: Lesson 6-9 — what the supply relay taught us
rows: If the divisor is less than 1, the quotient is bigger than the whole number. 8 ÷ ¼ must be more than 8.
8 ÷ ¼ asks how many ¼-meter clips fit in 8 meters. Each meter holds 4, so 8 × 4 = 32.
To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal: 9 ÷ ¾ = 9 × 4/3 = 12.
Multiply the quotient by the divisor: 25 × ⅖ = 10 and 6 × ⅔ = 4. You land back where you started.
Dividing does NOT always make things smaller. 10 ÷ ⅖ is 25, not 4.
journal.quote: "Dividing by a small piece makes a big answer. Dividing by Teo's confidence makes no answer at all." — Chip

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 6-9 (Divide Whole Numbers by Fractions) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: estimating before dividing, how many fractional pieces fit in a whole number, how much is in one whole, multiplying by the reciprocal, and checking by multiplying.
standards: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions; solve word problems involving division of fractions
